MP queries debt sustainability as Ngultrum falls

MP questioned whether the Ministry of Finance had carried out stress tests and repayment analyses under different INR-USD depreciation scenarios, and whether the government had a hedging framework in place to manage foreign exchange risks.

Lawmakers have raised concerns over growing currency risks associated with the country's non-hydropower external debt portfolio, warning that continued depreciation of the Ngultrum against the US dollar could increase the country's repayment burden in the future.

During Question Hour session in the National Assembly on May 22, the Member of Parliament for Gangzur-Minjay Loday Tsheten questioned the government on the sustainability of external debt, particularly loans denominated in US dollars and Special Drawing Rights (SDR)-linked currencies borrowed from multilateral institutions such as the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank.
The MP said that Bhutan indirectly inherits the depreciation pressures of the Indian Rupee because the Ngultrum is pegged to the Indian currency.

He questioned whether the Ministry of Finance had carried out stress tests and repayment analyses under different INR-USD depreciation scenarios, and whether the government had a hedging framework in place to manage foreign exchange risks.
According to the Debt Situation Report as of March 3, public debt stood at, equivalent to 90.6 percent of gross domestic product.
Hydropower-related debt accounted for 58.3 percent of external debt, while the remaining 41.7 percent was non-hydropower debt.

Finance Minister Lekey Dorji said that the debt portfolio remains sustainable under existing debt management frameworks, although the growing share of convertible currency-denominated debt requires close monitoring.
Lyonpo said Bhutan's external debt continues to be dominated by concessional borrowings supporting socio-economic development priorities.
He added that of the total convertible currency debt amounting to, approximately relates to non-hydropower external debt.
A substantial portion of this debt consists of concessional loans from multilateral development partners denominated in USD and SDR-linked currencies.

Finance Ministry regularly undertakes comprehensive debt assessments, including Debt Sustainability Analyses both internally and in collaboration with the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.
Additionally, the ministry conducts quarterly cost and risk indicator assessments to monitor vulnerabilities within the debt portfolio.
Regarding the possible impact of INR depreciation against the US Dollar,
Lyonpo said the government conducts scenario-based analyses and repayment projections under different exchange rate assumptions for internal policy and risk management purposes.
However, detailed repayment sensitivity estimates are not publicly disclosed.
According to Lyonpo, the government is also engaging with hedge and swap providers at the technical level to explore possible hedging transactions to manage foreign exchange exposure.
As part of this process, the government is assessing the institutional, policy, and operational frameworks Bhutan would need to effectively undertake such transactions, " he said.

Lyonpo said the ministry has already commenced contracting new debt from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the International Finance Corporation with provisions that include the option for cross-currency swap conversion.
This is expected to support the government’s broader efforts to strengthen external debt risk management and enhance resilience against exchange rate volatility.
He acknowledged that Bhutan's dependence on imports and the Ngultrum's peg to the Indian Rupee continue to expose the economy to external currency fluctuations.
Since the rupee is weakening against the US dollar, that is why fuel prices are increasing, " Lyonpo said.

He added that while the currency peg with India has supported Bhutan as an import-driven economy, the country also needs to improve its current account and trade balance to reduce external vulnerabilities.
We should not think that INR 100 is equivalent to when we import, " he said, calling for broader public understanding of Bhutan's external sector challenges.

The National Assembly today held the first and second readings of the Mutual Legal Assistance (MLA) in Criminal Matters Bill 2026 during the ongoing session.
The Home Minister presented the Bill to the House and received full support for its discussion.
Speaker Lungten Dorji directed the Human Rights and Foreign Relations Committee of the House to review the Bill and present it during the winter session for deliberation.
The Bill seeks to establish a comprehensive legal framework to strengthen cooperation between Bhutan and foreign countries in criminal investigations and proceedings.
It proposes mechanisms for providing legal assistance to foreign countries upon request and for Bhutan to seek similar assistance from other nations.
It also outlines the types of assistance that may be extended in response to incoming requests.

The proposed legislation further aims to ensure the admissibility of evidence transmitted to Bhutan through outgoing requests and to fulfil obligations arising from international conventions to which Bhutan is a party.

The Bill is considered necessary for the country, as both the National Assembly and the National Council have ratified the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC) Convention on Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters.
Without an MLA Act, it would not be possible to implement the BIMSTEC Convention on Mutual Legal Assistance.

Major investment commitments mark opening of BATIF 2.0

BATIF 2.0 was hosted by the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock (Mo AL) in partnership with the Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations (FAO), the Asian Development Bank (ADB), and the European Union.
Bhutan has secured major investment commitments and strategic partnerships worth billions of ngultrum, as the Bhutan Agrifood Trade and Investment Forum (BATIF) 2.0 opened in Thimphu today.

Marking a decisive push to transform the country’s agrifood sector through private and international investment, five major partnerships will be formalised tomorrow through Memoranda of Understanding (Mo Us).

BATIF 2.0 was hosted by the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock (Mo AL) in partnership with the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the Asian Development Bank (ADB), and the European Union.
The largest commitment came from a partnership between DAdvance Agarwood and Dheyma Harvest to strengthen vegetable supply chain and expand market access over the next 10 years.
The ADB has committed USD 2 million as catalytic financing support to the Bhutan Agri Sustain Fund (BAF), which was launched last year to accelerate agrifood transformation.
Japanese company Strout Inc. will support Bhutan in developing the trout value chain through land-based aquaculture expertise.

The Chaudhary Group will support market linkages for herbs, potatoes and essential oils, while also extending assistance in access to finance, incubation, acceleration and seed funding through partnerships with FAO Bhutan.
Another key partnership will see NOB Bhutan Farmers collaborate with the Mo AL,
Bhutan Development Bank Limited and FAO Bhutan to strengthen potato production, with an overall investment of.
Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay, who graced the forum as chief guest, said BATIF 2.0 was no longer about discussing possibilities, but about delivering action targeted towards farmers.
“Initially, we used to ask: Can Bhutan’s agrifood sector become something bigger?
Can it become more dynamic and transformational?” Lyonchhen said. “Now we can answer these questions.
Such forums are not about possibilities; it is about execution into actionable projects for our farmers.”

The government has proposed a budget of for the fiscal year 2026–27, representing 30 percent of the 13th Plan’s total outlay.
The allocation shows an increase of compared to the previous fiscal year’s revised budget of.
Presenting the annual budget report and Budget Appropriation Bill for the financial year 2026-27 in the National Assembly yesterday,

Finance Minister Lekey Dorji said the fiscal framework is anchored on the theme “Building Resilience and Self-Reliance, ” supported by a series of structural reforms aimed at strengthening Bhutan’s economic foundations.

“The budget aligns with Bhutan’s long-term economic transformation agenda, including the 10X national ambition and the development of Gelephu Mindfulness City as a strategic growth hub intended to attract investment and diversify the economy, ” Lyonpo said.
Out of the total proposed budget, is allocated for recurrent expenditure, for capital expenditure, for public debt principal repayment, and for on-lending.

According to the budget report, recurrent expenditure increased by 7.9 percent from the previous financial year, due to inflation adjustment of about 4 percent, onboarding of annual maintenance contracts for whole-of-government systems, allocation for the Population and Housing Census 2027, and conduct of the fourth local government elections.
Additionally, capital expenditure increased by 16 percent as the focus shifted from groundwork and preparatory activities to full-scale implementation.
Despite the positive growth outlook, the budget projects a fiscal deficit of, equivalent to 6.5 percent of GDP, making it one of the highest fiscal gaps recorded during the 13th Plan period so far.
The government expects total available resources of for the 2026–27 fiscal year.
Of this, domestic revenue is projected at, external grants at, and other receipts at.
Goods and Services Tax collections alone are estimated at, reflecting improved tax performance and a broader revenue base.

To finance the budget, the government expects domestic revenue to cover 72.1 percent of recurrent expenditure, underscoring efforts to reduce dependence on external financing and enhance fiscal self-reliance.
Domestic revenue is expected to be driven by indirect taxes, hydropower earnings, customs duties, dividends from state-owned enterprises, and tourism-related income.

The finance ministry projects the economy will grow moderately to 6.3 percent in 2026, primarily due to global economic headwinds, including geopolitical tensions in West Asia, commodity price volatility, and ongoing supply chain disruptions.
The larger GDP base in 2025 is also expected to contribute to a statistical slowdown in growth momentum in 2026.

However, medium-term projections show a recovery to 7.6 percent in 2027, driven by the industrial sector, hydropower expansion, construction activity, and the gradual revival of tourism and related services.

The unemployment rate is expected to decline slightly to 2.9 percent in 2026 before rising marginally to 3.1 percent in 2027, reflecting shifts in labour absorption as major infrastructure projects progress.

Gross international reserves are projected to improve significantly over the medium term, rising to USD 1.5 billion in fiscal year 2026–27 and further increasing to USD 1.54 billion in fiscal year 2027–28, equivalent to 39 months of import cover.

The health sector has been allocated, with a strong focus on expanding tertiary healthcare and improving service delivery.
Key investments include for a multi-disciplinary super-specialty hospital, for a mother and child hospital in Mongar, and infrastructure development for CT,
Regional hospitals in Samtse, Trashigang, and Phuentsholing will also be strengthened to improve equitable access to healthcare services.
A total of has been allocated for medical equipment and ambulances, and for the electronic Patient Information System and related digital health initiatives.
The education sector has received, one of the largest allocations in the budget.

Key investments include for developing 20 Phase I central school clusters, along with new institutions such as the International School in Thimphu and the STEM School at Drukgyel Higher Secondary School.
Curriculum reform aligned with the Cambridge framework has been allocated for implementation in Classes IX and XI, supported by teacher training, assessment reforms, and digitised learning materials.
Teacher development remains a priority, with allocated for training and leadership programmes.

The TVET sector receives for modernisation, while supports infrastructure expansion in technical institutes and resource centers.
Higher education is allocated for infrastructure, digital transformation, and international accreditation.
The Renewable Natural Resources (RNR) sector has been allocated to strengthen food security, rural livelihoods, and climate resilience.
Key investments include for irrigation development, for two Commercial Chirup Farms in Samrang and Pemathang, and for the Yarjugang Agriculture Commercial Farm.
To enhance resilience, has been allocated for the National Crop and Livestock Insurance Scheme, while will support market linkages and agribusiness development.
Additional funds include for export promotion, for farm shops, and for the Floriculture Centre of Excellence in Tsirang.
The sector also includes for sustainable forest management and allocations for biodiversity conservation and water resource inventory.

The energy sector has been allocated, focusing strongly on expanding renewable energy generation and strengthening long-term energy security in line with Bhutan’s transition toward a diversified energy mix.
It includes for a 1MW turbulent micro hydropower pilot project and for the ongoing 500k W hydropower project in Lunana.
Additional allocations include for solar photovoltaic systems in Wachey,
Lunana, and Shingphel, and for solar installations in three central schools.
The budget also allocates to establish a 1MW Green Hydrogen Refueling Station at Gidakom, marking a strategic step toward emerging clean energy technologies.
The sector has been allocated to enhance urban infrastructure, public utilities, and environmental resilience.
Key investments include for integrated water systems and for strengthening public transport services, including bus prioritisation and key urban corridors.
The budget also provides for green infrastructure and open spaces in Thimphu, including neighborhood parks.
Further allocations include for the expansion of Kaja Throm, for the construction of the Hongtsho Crematorium, for a Government Office Complex, and for the Gelephu flood mitigation project.
The transport sector has been allocated to strengthen national connectivity and improve road and air infrastructure.

A major portion of the budget is earmarked for road maintenance and improvement, including for routine maintenance, for dzongkhag roads, for Primary National Highways, and for Secondary National Highways.
Additional funds include for bridge construction and strengthening.
The allocation also includes to promote low-emission transport and electric vehicles, and for airport development to enhance air connectivity.

The government has allocated to the law and order services sector, covering the Royal Bhutan Police, the Judiciary, the Department of Law and Order under the Ministry of Home Affairs, and the Office of the Attorney General.

Of the total, has been earmarked as capital investment for the Royal Bhutan Police to enhance operational capacity in fire and rescue services, traffic enforcement, crime prevention, and rehabilitation programmes.
The Judiciary has been allocated to support infrastructure development, digital transformation, and human resource capacity building.

Major initiatives include the construction of the Thimphu Dzongkhag Court (Phase I) and strengthening digital justice systems such as the Case Management System and e-Litigation platform to improve efficiency and access to justice.
In addition, the Office of the Attorney General was allocated to enhance legal services, strengthen rights protection, and improve institutional readiness in addressing emerging legal challenges.
The government has allocated for human resource development, reflecting a continued emphasis on building a skilled and high-performing public service to support Bhutan’s long-term development vision.
The allocation covers training, capacity building, leadership development, scholarships, and talent development programs across the public sector.
Local governments have been allocated, marking a 23.6 percent increase from the previous fiscal year.
Of this, 62.3 percent is dedicated to capital expenditure, reflecting a strong emphasis on decentralised infrastructure development.

The general public services sector has been allocated to support the government’s core administrative and institutional functions, including constitutional bodies, the legislature, foreign missions, and local governance institutions.
